events.text: The first Votary of {b3_sect} is still here. The others came, learned the rites and went down to the villages. This one arrived the first winter with a bundle, and now sweeps the Hall of Offerings at dawn, and answers every question with a serene "it is as the god wills." You have not once been able to tell if this is faith or a fine way of not deciding.

choices.text: Ask the Votary what they themself want

effects.log: The Votary thinks for a long time and says: "to keep sweeping." You are not sure whether you have been taught or insulted.

choices.text: Send the Votary down to a village to keep a small shrine

effects.log: The Votary goes, unwillingly, and in a year sends word: the shrine is swept, the villagers are fed, and the Votary has opinions.

events.text: The Votary of {b3_sect} who would only sweep has, without warning, begun to preach. Not in the Hall: in the courtyard, at dusk, to the pilgrims queuing for the Gate of Incense. The sermons are short, plain and rather good. The senior Votaries are alarmed; they have not given leave. The pilgrims are rapt.

choices.text: Let the sweeper preach, and listen from the back

effects.log: You listen. The sermons are about sweeping, and the god, and not asking for anything. By the third dusk you are crying a little, at the back.

choices.text: Ask the sweeper to preach inside the Hall, with the rite, so that it is the Cult's

effects.log: You ask. The sweeper, appalled, agrees, and the sermons lose a little of their life and gain a lot of listeners.

events.text: A century on, the sweeper of {b3_sect} is the most beloved Votary the Cult has had, and the oldest. A pilgrim asks the sweeper, at the Gate, what the god wants. The sweeper answers at last: "for you to be gentle with yourselves." The queue is silent. The senior Votaries note it down. The sweeper goes back to the broom.

choices.text: Make "be gentle with yourselves" the first line of the Cult's doctrine

effects.log: You make it so. The Cult is thereafter known as the gentle one, and its pilgrims are, on the whole, kinder.

choices.text: Keep the doctrine as it is, and add the sweeper's line to the Book of Sayings

effects.log: You add it. The line is quoted for ages, and the sweeper, told, shrugs and sweeps.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_sect} has begun to answer questions with questions. A pilgrim asks whether the harvest will fail; the Pool asks what the pilgrim has done with last year's seed. The Votaries are mortified, and the pilgrims, after a pause, find it oddly helpful. The Pool has an air of enjoying itself.

choices.text: Let the Pool ask, and train the Votaries to hear the question inside the question

effects.log: You let it. The Votaries learn to read the Pool's riddles, and the pilgrims go home with better questions than they came with.

choices.text: Rebuke the Pool, gently, and ask it to answer plainly

effects.log: You rebuke it. The Pool sulks for a month, and then answers plainly, and the answers are rather dull.

events.text: The Pool of {b3_sect} has asked you a question, unprompted: "what would you do if you did not have to be a god?" The Hall is empty. The water is perfectly still. You realise this is the question the Pool has been working up to for centuries, through the pilgrims. It waits, glittering, with absurd patience.

choices.text: Answer it honestly, aloud, to the water

effects.log: You answer. The Pool takes it in, without a ripple, and then says: "I have been wondering the same." You sit with it a long while.

choices.text: Turn the question back and ask what the Pool would do

effects.log: The Pool answers: "be rain." You think about it for a decade.

events.text: The Pool of {b3_sect} has asked to be allowed to rain. Not as a pool: as rain, on the dry lands to the west, for a season. It would leave the Cult unanswered for a time. The Votaries are dismayed. The pilgrims, if they knew, would be bereft. The western lands, in drought, have been praying a long time, and the Pool has heard.

choices.text: Grant the request, and place a plain bowl of water in the Hall for the season

effects.log: You grant it. The Pool goes, a shimmer, and the west greens, and the bowl in the Hall answers pilgrims in single words.

choices.text: Refuse, and send a herald with a sack of water to the west instead

effects.log: You refuse. The herald brings what he can, and the west is helped a little, and the Pool sulks in the Hall.

events.text: A quarrel has split the Votaries of {b3_sect} into two benches. One holds that the god has one flame; the other that the god has two. The one-flame bench points to the oldest hymn. The two-flame bench points to the glyph above the Gate, which has, they say, two. Both appeal to you, who founded the Cult, to say how many flames it has.

choices.text: Say you do not remember, and that the Cult is wiser than its founder

effects.log: You say so. The benches stare, then laugh, shaken by honesty, and the quarrel loses some of its edge.

choices.text: Rule for one flame, as the oldest hymn says

effects.log: You rule so. The two-flame bench withdraws, grave and wounded, to a corner of the Hall.

choices.text: Rule for two, as the glyph shows

effects.log: You rule so. The one-flame bench retires to the gate-house to keep a single lamp, in silence.

events.text: The two benches of {b3_sect} have not spoken in a decade. The Cult is divided in the Hall, in the refectory, and in the choir. A pilgrim, a tired old farmer, has been walking between the benches with a pot of tea, and nobody has been able to stop him. He pours for both. He says he does not care how many flames there are, only that the tea is hot.

choices.text: Invite the farmer to speak to both benches at once

effects.log: You invite him. He says three sentences, and the benches, mortified, sit down at the same table, and the tea is hot.

choices.text: Ask the benches to count the flames together, in the Hall, at night

effects.log: You ask. They count, and there are two, and one, and neither, depending on where you stand, and the quarrel ends in awed confusion.

events.text: A thousand years after the Quarrel of the Flames, {b3_sect} has a feast of the Tea, held in the courtyard on the night the benches first sat together. It is the Cult's dearest rite. A child asks a Votary how many flames the god has. The Votary starts to answer, stops, and laughs. "Come and see," the Votary says, and takes the child to the Hall.

choices.text: Follow the Votary and the child, and watch

effects.log: You follow. In the Hall, in the dark, the Votary lights a lamp and lets the child see it twice, once in the glass, once on the wall. The child understands at once.

choices.text: Let the Votary teach alone, and stay at the feast

effects.log: You stay at the feast. The tea is hot, and the laughter reaches the Hall from the dark, and the Cult is whole.

events.text: The Gate of Incense of {b3_sect} is smoking a different colour. Pilgrims in the queue mutter that it is an omen. The head Votary says the censer-boy mixed the cedar with something else. The censer-boy, nine hundred years old and mortified, offers to confess. The smoke is a lovely, lazy lavender, and is being admired by passers-by.

choices.text: Keep the lavender, and call it the Gate's new colour

effects.log: You keep it. The Gate becomes known across the district as the lilac gate, and pilgrims come for the smell.

choices.text: Have the censer-boy mix the old cedar again, and forgive him

effects.log: You forgive him. The cedar returns, severe and fine, and the censer-boy, grateful, never errs again.

events.text: A Votary of {b3_sect} has been caught giving away the Hall of Offerings' ceremonial rice to hungry pilgrims, bowl by bowl, out of a side door. The chief Votary wants an example made. The pilgrims are hungry. The Votary, young and appalled at being found out, holds the empty bowl in both hands.

choices.text: Make the side door official, and call it the Door of Bread

effects.log: You do. The Door of Bread becomes the Cult's best-known work, and the young Votary is promoted to its keeper.

choices.text: Rebuke the Votary mildly and order a ration set for pilgrims

effects.log: You rebuke, and set a ration. The pilgrims eat smaller, steady portions, and the Votary is relieved.

events.text: The doctrines of {b3_sect} have grown in the telling. What began as three sentences is now a library of commentaries. The Votaries cite them at each other like swords. A young acolyte, asked to summarise the Cult's creed, says: "it is a lot of people being very polite about a candle." The room is silent. The chief Votary, to everyone's surprise, laughs.

choices.text: Ask the acolyte to write that sentence into the opening of the creed

effects.log: The acolyte, aghast, writes it. The creed, thereafter, begins with a joke, and is read more often than before.

choices.text: Thank the acolyte, and commission a short creed of nine lines for the young

effects.log: You commission it. The short creed is learned by every child in the district, and is, to the Votaries' chagrin, the best thing the Cult has written.

events.text: A pilgrim of {b3_sect} has come to the Hall of Offerings with a very strange offering: a stone, gray, ordinary, wrapped in a woollen scarf. The pilgrim says it is their grandmother. The Votaries are scandalised. The pilgrim, calmly, says that their grandmother, when dying, asked to be made a stone, so as to keep still for a while.

choices.text: Place the stone on the altar, beside the lamps, with a small rite

effects.log: You do. The stone sits with the lamps, grave and lovely, and pilgrims bring their own, and the Hall acquires a quiet row of the beloved.

choices.text: Take the stone into the Cult's garden, where it can sit in the sun

effects.log: You take it. The garden fills, in time, with stones, and a few wildflowers, and the Cult is known as gentle.

events.text: It is the Feast of the Lamp in {b3_sect}, and the head Votary has fallen ill. The Cult must light its Great Lamp at dusk, with the rite. Nobody else knows the words. The head Votary is in bed, fever-bright, dictating them to a scribe. The scribe is too slow. Dusk is a quarter of an hour away. You are holding the taper.

choices.text: Light the Lamp yourself, saying what you remember of the rite

effects.log: You light it. The words you remember are not quite the words, but the Lamp catches, and the Votaries, hearing a plain version, find it more moving than the true one.

choices.text: Carry the taper to the sickbed, and have the head Votary light it by hand

effects.log: You carry it. The head Votary lights it with a shaking hand, and the Lamp is lit at the bedside, and the Cult files past, weeping.

events.text: Two pilgrims arrive at {b3_sect} on the same night, from opposite directions, each claiming to have been called by a dream. The dreams are, when compared, the same dream. Each pilgrim was told to bring a gift to the other. They stand in the courtyard exchanging parcels in bewilderment. The parcels contain, each, half of a broken lamp.

choices.text: Join the halves in the Hall, and light the mended lamp

effects.log: You join them. The lamp, whole, burns a soft green, and the Cult adds it to its altar.

choices.text: Ask the pilgrims what they were told the lamp was for

effects.log: They tell you, in two voices, taking turns, and the answer is a short, wise sentence about the Cult itself.

events.text: The Warden of the Gate of Incense of {b3_sect} has taken to turning away pilgrims at random. Not cruelly: with a bow, a smile and a gentle "not today." The pilgrims, astounded, come back the next week, and the next, and are admitted after three attempts, wiser and humbler. The Warden says it is a spiritual discipline. The chief Votary says it is a nuisance.

choices.text: Let the Warden continue, and bring the custom into the rite

effects.log: You let him. The custom is added to the rite, "the Three Turnings," and the pilgrims prize it.

choices.text: Ask the Warden to give each refused pilgrim a cup of tea and a reason

effects.log: You ask. The reasons are baffling and the tea is good, and the Gate is, thereafter, a sort of friendly puzzle.

events.text: A young Votary of {b3_sect} has been writing hymns in a modern idiom, with rhymes and a tune. The old Votaries are horrified. The pilgrims, hearing them in the courtyard, sing along. The hymns are about turnips, grief and the weather. One of them is, by general admission, devastating. The young Votary asks only to sing them at dawn.

choices.text: Let the young Votary sing them at dawn, and add the best to the Cult's book

effects.log: You let them. The best is added, and sung by the whole district for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask the young Votary to teach the old Votaries the tunes, a verse a week

effects.log: You ask. The old Votaries grumble and hum, and by spring the Hall is full of turnip hymns.

events.text: A pestilence of mice has invaded the Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect}. The Votaries want them poisoned. The mice, in a body, have taken up residence under the altar and refuse to leave. The Cult's doctrine is that all creatures may take shelter at the altar. A mouse, bold and bright-eyed, sits on the lamp-stand, and looks at you.

choices.text: Honour the doctrine: leave the mice and set out a dish of grain

effects.log: You do. The mice become, in time, the Cult's unofficial choir, and are tolerated with a shrug.

choices.text: Persuade the mice to move to the granary with a better dish

effects.log: You persuade them. The mice move, and the granary prospers, and the Hall is quiet.

events.text: The Cult of {b3_sect} has a relic, a bowl said to have belonged to its first Votary. A scholar of the Hall of Names visits and says, with regret, that the bowl is a thousand years too young. The Votaries are devastated. The pilgrims, hearing of it, bring the bowl offerings anyway. The scholar sits, watching, with a puzzled expression.

choices.text: Declare the bowl the Cult's relic of devotion, not of origin

effects.log: You declare it. The bowl is kept, and the pilgrims, at the story, shrug and love it more.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to find the real bowl, and give them a year to search

effects.log: You ask. The search takes a century, and finds a shard, and the shard is placed in the new bowl, and both are cherished.

events.text: A famine of belief has struck {b3_sect}. The pilgrims have dwindled to a trickle. The Hall of Offerings is half empty. The Votaries, in the evenings, sing to nobody. The head Votary comes to you at night, grey, and asks whether the Cult should close the Gate for a season, and be silent, and wait. It is not a suggestion. It is a plea for permission to stop.

choices.text: Close the Gate for a season, and tell the Votaries to rest

effects.log: You close it. The Votaries sleep, and eat, and walk in the hills, and return in the spring renewed, and the pilgrims return in the summer.

choices.text: Keep the Gate open, but send the Votaries out to the villages to go to the people

effects.log: You send them. The Votaries are scattered and weary, and the villagers, meeting them, rediscover the Cult.

events.text: A mortal king has asked {b3_sect} to bless his new fleet. The fleet is bound for conquest. The Cult has no doctrine against it; it has no doctrine for it, either. The king has sent a hundred jars of oil and a poem. The head Votary, torn, says the Cult has never been asked to bless a war, and does not know the words.

choices.text: Refuse, courteously, and send the oil to the poor

effects.log: You refuse. The king, startled, takes it in a cold silence, and a year later, sheepishly, sends more oil with no request.

choices.text: Bless the sailors, not the fleet, in a short rite of safe return

effects.log: You bless them. The king accepts with a growl, and the sailors return safe, and the war, in the end, is a smaller one.

events.text: A traveller god has stopped at the Gate of {b3_sect} and, to the Votaries' delight, recognised the Cult as the successor of a very old tradition, the Cult of the Lamp Before the Lamp, long extinct. They offer to teach the Votaries the lost rites. They are charming and persuasive. The head Votary, who has her doubts, watches.

choices.text: Accept the lost rites, in a trial season, with the head Votary's doubts noted

effects.log: You accept. The rites are strange and lovely, and the head Votary, at the season's end, concedes they are real, and takes notes.

choices.text: Thank the traveller and ask for the rites in writing to be examined by scholars

effects.log: You ask. The scholars take a decade, and the rites are largely authentic, and the Cult adopts a few.

events.text: On the longest night, a child is found asleep in the Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect}, curled at the foot of the altar. No one knows where it came from. It has the faint glow of something newly made. When it wakes, it says only: "I am the Cult's," and asks for breakfast. The Votaries confer in whispers. Nobody knows what the child is.

choices.text: Take the child in as a ward of the Cult, and ask nothing

effects.log: You take it in. The child grows, in a century, into a quiet attendant of the Hall, with an odd gift for finding lost things.

choices.text: Ask the Oracle Pool what the child is

effects.log: The Pool answers: "yours." You are not sure whether it means the Cult, or you.

events.text: The Cult of {b3_sect} has been invited to take part in a council of the cults of the district, where the cults will agree a common calendar of feasts. The other cults are older, richer and more numerous. The Cult's delegate, the sweeper, goes in a patched robe with a flask of tea and no instructions. You wait, fretful.

choices.text: Send word to the sweeper: trust yourself, and say what the Cult believes

effects.log: You send it. The sweeper returns, three weeks later, with a calendar in which the Cult's feast of the Tea is the central one.

choices.text: Send an escort of senior Votaries to stand behind the sweeper

effects.log: You send them. The council is impressed, and the calendar is a compromise, and the sweeper is a little hurt.

events.text: Pilgrims of {b3_sect} have reported seeing the god of the Cult, in their dreams, wearing a hat. The hat is red, and floppy, and slightly ridiculous. The god, in the dreams, is reading a newspaper. The Votaries are in a state. It is not the traditional iconography. It is, nevertheless, the same dream, from forty pilgrims, in the same week.

choices.text: Adopt the hat, and add it to the Cult's iconography

effects.log: You adopt it. The red hat becomes the Cult's sign, and every child in the district draws it.

choices.text: Ask the Oracle Pool why the god wears a hat

effects.log: The Pool ripples with something that is clearly laughter, and answers: "for the wind." The Votaries decide this is profound.

events.text: A funeral at {b3_sect}, for a pilgrim who died on the stair of dawn, with no family. The Votaries lay the body in the Hall and keep vigil. By midnight, nine hundred strangers have come to stand in the dark, quietly, having heard that someone died alone. Nobody has called them. The vigil flames burn steady.

choices.text: Stay the night with the strangers, and say the pilgrim's name aloud at dawn

effects.log: You stay. The name is spoken nine hundred times by dawn, and the pilgrim, you feel, would have been astonished.

choices.text: Open the refectory and feed the strangers

effects.log: You feed them. The meal is quiet and long, and the strangers leave at dawn with the Cult's blessing.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_sect} has been used for centuries to answer questions of the future, and a hardy Votary has discovered that it can also answer questions about the past. A pilgrim asks whether his father loved him. The Pool answers. The pilgrim weeps. The Votaries are divided: should the Cult be in the business of answering such questions?

choices.text: Allow the Pool to answer questions of the past, with a Votary present for comfort

effects.log: You allow it. The Pool becomes a place of long pilgrimage and a lot of tissue.

choices.text: Keep the Pool to the future, and send the past-seekers to the scribes

effects.log: You keep it so. The scribes are overwhelmed and kind, and the Pool is a less emotional place.

events.text: A band of wandering players arrives at {b3_sect} and asks leave to perform in the courtyard. They bring a masque of the god of the Cult, with a mask, a cape and a great deal of smoke. The head Votary, aghast, sees that the god in the masque is rather short and bad-tempered, and rather good. The pilgrims, watching, roar.

choices.text: Let them perform, and ask for a repeat for the Feast

effects.log: You let them. The masque is staged at the Feast every year thereafter, and the god, you suspect, is entertained.

choices.text: Let them perform, but ask for the god's temper to be softened

effects.log: You ask. The players soften it, a little, and the masque is more tender, and still funny.

events.text: The lamp-oil of {b3_sect} has been tampered with: a few drops of something sweet have been added. The lamps burn a faint pink. The Votaries are in a rage, looking for the culprit. A small god of sweets, visiting, is found asleep in the oil store, sticky, blissful and unrepentant. He says he thought it would improve the scent.

choices.text: Forgive the little god of sweets and ask for the recipe

effects.log: You forgive him. The pink lamps become the Cult's festival lights, and he is made keeper of them, and is insufferable.

choices.text: Banish the sweet oil from the Hall, and give the god a dish of honey as a peace

effects.log: You banish it. The god, comforted with honey, leaves, and the oil is plain again.

events.text: An old god, a very old god, one of the first of the Elder Lineages, has come to {b3_sect} on pilgrimage. He will not say why. He sits in the Hall for nine days, in the dark, without speaking. On the tenth he rises, bows to the altar, and says: "I used to pray here, when it was a field." He leaves a single stone at the door.

choices.text: Place the stone on the altar, and tell the Votaries its story

effects.log: You place it. The Votaries learn that the Cult stands on an older ground, and it changes how they sweep.

choices.text: Ask the old god to come again, and promise a field of his own beside the Hall

effects.log: You ask. He comes again, and you plant a field, and he sits in it, content.

events.text: A scribe of {b3_sect} has discovered an error in the Cult's calendar: it has been a day out for four hundred years. Every feast has been kept on the wrong day. The head Votary is stricken. The scribe is trembling. The pilgrims, if told, will be upset. The god of the Cult, if asked, would shrug. The calendar is, in any case, very beautiful.

choices.text: Correct the calendar, and keep one feast on the old day as a memorial

effects.log: You correct it. The memorial feast, on the wrong day, becomes the Cult's favourite.

choices.text: Leave the calendar as it is; the day is the Cult's own now

effects.log: You leave it. The scribe, relieved, keeps the secret, and the Cult is, charmingly, always a day late.

events.text: A crow has taken up residence on the roof of the Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect}, and steals, daily, one small thing from the altar. The Votaries find the objects, in a heap, in the belfry. The crow is clearly a minor spirit, with a collector's eye. It is looking at you now, from the beam, with a gleam in its eye, holding your spectacles.

choices.text: Make a trade: a shiny bead for the spectacles, every week

effects.log: You make it. The crow keeps its side, and the heap in the belfry grows into a small, curious museum.

choices.text: Ask the Votaries to set a decoy on the altar, a bright, worthless trinket

effects.log: You do. The crow takes the decoy for a year, and the altar is safe, and the crow is content.

events.text: Pilgrims climbing to {b3_sect} must pass a shrine halfway, kept by a cheerful, ancient priestess. Lately she has been charging a fee. It is small: a song, a pinch of salt, a funny story. The pilgrims love it. The Votaries think it undignified. The priestess says the stair is long and she is lonely. She says it is not a toll; it is a conversation.

choices.text: Let the priestess keep her songs and stories, and add a bench and a lamp

effects.log: You add them. The halfway shrine becomes the most beloved stop on the stair, and the Votaries come to visit.

choices.text: Ask her gently to make it a gift, with no fee

effects.log: You ask. She laughs, and agrees, and says it was always a gift, only now the pilgrims will not leave.

events.text: The Cult of {b3_sect} has been given a bell. It came by cart, with no sender, wrapped in oilcloth, and a note: "for the day it is needed." The bell is a fine one, with a deep voice. The Votaries do not know what to do with it. They hang it in the belfry and do not ring it. Every night it hums, very faintly, in anticipation.

choices.text: Ring the bell once, on a quiet day, to see what comes

effects.log: You ring it. Nothing comes. But the whole district, for a moment, stops what it is doing and looks up, and smiles.

choices.text: Keep it silent, and wait for the day it is needed

effects.log: You keep it. The bell hums, patiently, through the years, and the Votaries sleep a little lighter.

events.text: The Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect} has a ceiling painted by a god of colour, nine thousand years ago, in a single night. It depicts the sky as the Cult believes it ought to be. Lately the paint has begun to flake. A great flake falls on a pilgrim, who is delighted and calls it a blessing. The head Votary wishes to restore it. The god of colour, summoned, says he does not remember painting it.

choices.text: Ask the god of colour to repaint it, freshly, as he sees it now

effects.log: He does. It takes nine nights, and the new sky is different, wilder, and the Cult loves it.

choices.text: Have the Votaries restore the old one, flake by flake, with great care

effects.log: You do. It takes a century, and the old sky returns, a little paler, and holds.

events.text: A pilgrim at {b3_sect} asks the Votaries for a private audience with the god of the Cult. The Votaries explain that the god does not give audiences. The pilgrim, politely, asks again. And again. For nine days. On the tenth the Hall is full of other pilgrims, all asking, politely, for an audience. The god of the Cult, who is you, is wondering what to do.

choices.text: Grant the audience, in the Hall, to all of them at once

effects.log: You grant it. You sit in the Hall, and they sit, and nobody says anything, and it is the best audience of the age.

choices.text: Send a dream to each, and answer them privately, one by one

effects.log: You send them. Each pilgrim wakes with a small word in their heart, and the Hall empties peacefully.

events.text: An envoy of the Silent Hall has come to {b3_sect} to inspect the Cult, quietly, for the Book of Fates. The envoy, a pale god, sits at the back of the Hall for a week. The Votaries, terrified, are on their best behaviour. The envoy writes nothing. At the week's end, the envoy says, in a whisper, "you are doing it right," and leaves a feather on the altar.

choices.text: Keep the feather in the Hall, and say nothing of the inspection

effects.log: You keep it. The Votaries never learn what was written, and the feather is, to them, a sign.

choices.text: Tell the Votaries the envoy's words, and let them rejoice

effects.log: You tell them. The Hall rings with an unusual cheer, and the Cult is the lighter for it.

events.text: A famous poet has come to {b3_sect} to write a long work about the Cult. The poet stays a year. The poem, when finished, is magnificent, in thirty cantos, and entirely wrong about everything the Cult believes. The Votaries are enchanted by it. The pilgrims quote it. The doctrines of the Cult begin to drift toward the poem.

choices.text: Embrace the poem as the Cult's second scripture, errors and all

effects.log: You embrace it. The Cult grows lovelier and a little more inaccurate, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Ask the poet to add a thirty-first canto setting the facts straight, in verse

effects.log: The poet does, with humour. The canto is the best of the thirty-one, and the Cult is, again, itself.

events.text: A young god of a small domain asks to join {b3_sect} as a Votary. He is polite, nervous, and clearly in some trouble. He will not say what. He sleeps in the hall at night with a lamp lit. By the third week it is clear that he is hiding from something that will come in the dark. A sound comes to the Gate at night: patient, slow, regular.

choices.text: Sit up with him at the Gate, and meet whatever comes

effects.log: You sit up. What comes is a very old debt-collector, a tidy god of ledgers, who has been after him for six hundred years, and you negotiate.

choices.text: Hide him in the deepest cellar and send word to the Silent Hall

effects.log: You hide him. The Silent Hall sends an arbiter, and the matter is settled in court, and he is free.

events.text: The Cult of {b3_sect} holds a yearly Day of Doubt, on which the Votaries are permitted to say aloud anything they doubt about the god, the Cult, or themselves. It is the most popular day of the year. This year, a Votary of great age stands and says, trembling: "I have never believed in the god, and have served for eight thousand years." The Hall is silent.

choices.text: Embrace the Votary, and thank them for the truth

effects.log: You embrace them. The Hall exhales, and a dozen Votaries rise to say the same, and the Day of Doubt is the Cult's most honest rite.

choices.text: Ask the Votary what keeps them serving

effects.log: The Votary answers: "the people." The Hall nods, one by one, and the Cult is the stronger for it.

events.text: The Votaries of the Cult that has come under {b3_sect} are very correct. They bow, offer tea, present their Cult's Book of Offerings, and leave a space at the end of the row where your seal will go. Their eyes are polite and shuttered. You understand that you are being given everything except what you wanted, which was to be liked.

choices.text: Ask the elder Votaries to stay on as your counsellors, not your subjects

effects.log: They look at one another. The eldest says: "we will try." It takes a decade, and in the end they are your best advisers.

choices.text: Keep the Book, return the seal, and ask nothing more for a year

effects.log: You return it. The Votaries are bewildered, and in a year the first of them asks if they might, after all, use it.

events.text: A young Votary of the Cult brought under {b3_sect} arrives at the Hall of Offerings with a bundle and a hostile look. They have been sent to learn what you did, and to hate it. They are given a bed in the dormitory and a bowl of porridge. Within a week they have been absorbed into a card game, and within a month, the hating has become an argument about the best verse of a hymn.

choices.text: Invite the young Votary to your table and ask what they want to learn

effects.log: You ask. They want to know how a Cult can be gentle and strong. You answer, honestly, that it cannot be both at once, and that is the lesson.

choices.text: Leave them to the card game and its consequences

effects.log: You leave them. They learn more, probably, from the game, and the hymn.

events.text: The rival Cult's sacred lamp has been carried into the Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect} in procession, as the terms of the peace require. It is a small, blackened thing, very old. The rival Cult weeps as it is set among your lamps. The lamp, to your surprise, is lit. It burns with a smoky, sullen flame that does not match the others.

choices.text: Let the rival lamp burn as it is, in the place of honour

effects.log: You let it. The mismatched flame becomes the Hall's oldest and best-loved, and the rival Votaries visit it with proprietary tenderness.

choices.text: Ask the rival Votaries to teach your lamp-keepers how to trim it

effects.log: You ask. The lesson is slow, and the lamp burns brighter by the end, and the Cults are, for a while, a single trade.

events.text: The rival Cult that you have brought to heel has begun to leave anonymous notes in the Hall of Offerings of {b3_sect}: scraps of vellum with a single sentence each. "The incense is wrong." "You hold the bowl too high." "Our god would not have liked the stair." They are not hostile. They are the grief of a people who cannot say it aloud.

choices.text: Answer each note in writing, and leave the answers at the same spot

effects.log: You answer. The exchange goes on for years, and becomes the Cult's book of friendly correction, and the grief eases.

choices.text: Call the Cults together at the Gate and ask them to say it aloud

effects.log: You call them. The aloud is awful and necessary, and by the end the rival Votaries are in tears and in your arms.

events.text: The head of the Cult you brought to heel has come to {b3_sect} to offer their sword, in the old fashion, hilt first. They are a stern god, with grey in the beard and a face like a stone. The Votaries gather. The head kneels. They are shaking very slightly. It is the first time they have knelt in four thousand years.

choices.text: Take the sword and return it, hilt first, and raise them up

effects.log: You return it. The head stands, tears on their face, and swears an oath that is meant, and the Cult is yours.

choices.text: Accept the sword and keep it in the Hall as the Cults' common relic

effects.log: You keep it. The head, relieved of the weight, kneels a little longer than necessary, and is helped to rise.

events.text: Pilgrims of the rival Cult, now yours, have begun to arrive at the Gate of Incense of {b3_sect} in a continuous stream. They are lost: their own shrines were closed under the peace. They stand in the queue, bewildered, with the offerings of a dead habit in their hands. The Votaries do not know how to receive people whose god has changed hands.

choices.text: Open the Gate to them without a fee or a rite, and say welcome

effects.log: You open it. The pilgrims enter in a silent wave, and the Hall is, that week, the busiest in the district.

choices.text: Have the Votaries of both Cults greet them together at the Gate

effects.log: You arrange it. The greeting is awkward, and the pilgrims are moved, and a custom is born.

events.text: A hymn of the rival Cult has been sung by mistake at the dedication of a shrine of {b3_sect}, and has gone over rather well. The rival Votaries are embarrassed and moved. Your own Votaries are annoyed, then intrigued. The hymn has a third verse that no hymn of yours has ever had, about the last light of the day. The congregation sang it with all their hearts.

choices.text: Adopt the hymn as the Cults' common one, and sing it at the next Feast

effects.log: You adopt it. The rival Votaries weep, the Hall sings, and the hymn is sung in both Cults for ten thousand years.

choices.text: Ask the rival Votaries to write a new hymn with yours, a joint one

effects.log: You ask. The hymn is written over a year, and is a mixed, odd and beautiful thing.

events.text: The rival Cult's oracle, a blind old god, has come to live in the gate-house of {b3_sect} under the terms of the peace. He sits by the fire, silent, and listens to the Hall. On the first night he says, to nobody: "you speak differently here." The Votaries edge away. On the second night he says: "I like it."

choices.text: Sit by him one evening and ask what he hears in the Hall

effects.log: He tells you. It is an odd, lovely account of echoes and footsteps and the grain of the wood, and you hear your own Hall for the first time.

choices.text: Ask the Oracle Pool to speak to him, as one oracle to another

effects.log: The Pool ripples, and he answers, and the two talk through the night in a language of water.

events.text: The senior Votaries of {b3_sect} and of the Cult brought under it have fallen out over the seating at the Feast. Each insists on the place at the high table by right of ancestry. The rival Cult was, by its own account, older. Your Cult was, by its own, better. The quarrel has been going for nine days. The Feast is tomorrow. The food is cooling.

choices.text: Propose a round table, with no head, in the courtyard

effects.log: You propose it. The Votaries, baffled, assent, and sit, and the Feast is the least formal and most joyous the Cults have had.

choices.text: Seat the eldest of both at the high table, back to back

effects.log: You seat them. They sit, sulking, and by the third course are passing the salt.

events.text: The god of the rival Cult, brought to heel, has not been seen since the peace. The Votaries say the god has withdrawn, in grief or pride, to a high place. The people of the district, once of the rival Cult, ask whether they may still pray. The question is quiet, polite and terrible. You are asked to decide on behalf of both Cults whether a god may be forgotten by order.

choices.text: Declare that no god is forgotten by order, and that prayers may go where they please

effects.log: You declare it. The people pray as they will, and the rival god, in the high place, comes down a little, and listens.

choices.text: Go yourself to the high place, and ask the rival god to come down

effects.log: You climb. The rival god is old, tired, and unexpectedly kind, and you sit with them a while, and they agree.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the road with a scar across one hand, a bag of petitions, and a small, stubborn jar of something that smells of old trees. {He} sets the jar on your desk and says it was given by a mortal who would not give a name. {He} says it must be opened under a particular moon. {He} cannot say which.

choices.text: Open it under tonight's moon and see

effects.log: You open it. Inside is a seed, and a note: "for the god who sent the herald." The seed, planted, grows into a small, splendid, silver tree.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the whole story of the jar

effects.log: {npc} tells it, and it is long, and tender, and a little absurd, and the jar is kept sealed on the shelf as a keepsake.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with an unexpected companion: a young person from a far-off shrine, who has followed {him} home in the hope of becoming a Votary. {He} did not invite them. {He} says they were persistent, and also that they carried the bags the whole way. The newcomer stands at the Gate of Incense holding a battered umbrella and trying not to look hopeful.

choices.text: Admit the newcomer as a guest of the Cult for a season

effects.log: You admit them. By the end of the season they are the best sweeper in the Hall, and have named the umbrella.

choices.text: Send the newcomer home with a letter and a blessing

effects.log: You send them. They go, disappointed, and return a year later with a better umbrella and a better case.

events.text: {npc} is back from the road with news: a god in a far domain has been telling the mortals that {b3_sect} is a fraud. The accusation is vague and loud. {npc} has the details. The god is clever, well-liked and wrong in a particular, convincing way. {npc}, to your surprise, is not angry, only sad, and asks what you want done.

choices.text: Send {npc} back with a letter inviting the accuser to visit the Cult

effects.log: You send {him}. The accuser visits, and sees, and the accusations stop, with a grumpy letter of apology.

choices.text: Let the accusation run its course, and send {npc} to tend the nearest shrines

effects.log: You let it. The accusation fades, and {npc} tends the shrines, and the Cult is, a little, more loved.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the road with an armful of small gifts from the people of the villages: a loaf, a carved bird, a jar of honey, a baby's sock. {He} spreads them on your desk with the air of someone setting out a collection of stones. Each came with a message. {He} has memorised them all. {He} begins with the sock.

choices.text: Listen to every message, in the order {he} gives them

effects.log: You listen. It takes the night, and in the dawn you know the district better than any map, and the sock goes on the altar.

choices.text: Choose three of the gifts to keep on the altar, and thank {npc} for the rest

effects.log: You choose three. {npc} nods, understanding, and the other gifts are shared among the Votaries.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road thin, brown and silent, and does not say what happened. {He} sits in the Hall and watches the vigil flames with an unwavering gaze. After three days, {he} speaks: "I met someone." {He} will say no more. {He} wants to go back, soon, to look for them. {He} asks only for your leave.

choices.text: Grant leave, and give {him} a lamp to carry

effects.log: You grant it. {npc} goes, with the lamp, and returns in a year with a companion and a new quiet in {his} voice.

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you what {he} can about the one {he} met

effects.log: {npc} tells you, haltingly, and it is the saddest and most hopeful account of a meeting, and you give leave at once.

events.text: {npc} comes back from the road with a petition from a village that wants a shrine of {b3_sect}. The village is small, poor and remote. It has no priest. It has a roof, a hill, and a well. It wants a bowl, a lamp, and a Votary. {npc} supports the petition with a speech that goes on for some time, and is, in the end, rather moving.

choices.text: Grant the shrine, and send {npc} back with a bowl, a lamp and a young Votary

effects.log: You grant it. {npc} goes, and in time the village becomes a favourite stop for pilgrims, and {he} is its patron.

choices.text: Grant a visiting priest for the season, and promise a shrine when the village is ready

effects.log: You grant it. The season goes well, and the shrine is built the next year, and the village glows.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with a prisoner. Not a prisoner: a guest, {he} says, who happens to have been caught stealing offerings from a roadside shrine. The thief is a ragged boy-god of the crossroads, nine hundred years old, with an impressive scowl. {npc} says the boy-god was hungry. The boy-god says no. The stomach of the boy-god disagrees.

choices.text: Give the boy-god a meal and a place in the kitchens, and no scolding

effects.log: You do. The boy-god scowls through three helpings, and stays, and in a year is the Cult's best cook.

choices.text: Ask the boy-god why the stealing, and what would be done instead

effects.log: You ask. The boy-god says: "I would give things away." You give the boy-god a basket and a road, and the boy-god becomes a Votary of giving.

events.text: {npc} comes in from the road covered in dust, and carrying a mortal child on {his} back, asleep. {He} found the child at a shrine of {b3_sect} in the hills, alone, having walked three days to find the god of the Cult. The child has come to ask for a cure for a sick mother. {npc} looks at you over the child's head, pleadingly.

choices.text: Send {npc} back with the child and a healing herb, and a dream of the cure

effects.log: You send them. The mother recovers, and the child, grown, returns as a Votary of healing.

choices.text: Go yourself, in disguise, with {npc}, to the mother's bedside

effects.log: You go. The mother is saved, and the child never knows who sat at the bedside, but remembers the kindness.

events.text: {npc} has returned from the road with a disquieting rumour: a rival Cult of the same domain is forming far to the east, with a better hymn, a younger god and a simpler doctrine. Its pilgrims are already crossing the mountains. {npc} does not know whether to be alarmed or admiring. {He} has brought back one of the hymns, written on a leaf.

choices.text: Read the hymn aloud in the Hall, and judge it fairly

effects.log: You read it. It is, indeed, better than yours in places, and the Hall is silent, and then someone suggests learning it.

choices.text: Send {npc} east again, with a letter of friendship to the rival Cult

effects.log: You send {him}. The letter is received with surprise, and the two Cults, in time, trade pilgrims and hymns.

events.text: {npc} returns, dishevelled, laughing, with a long story about a feast at a crossroads shrine where the local god mistook {him} for a sacrifice and tried to eat {him}, then discovered {he} was a herald and apologised so profusely that {he} had to console the god. {He} has a gift: a pot of exceedingly strong plum wine. {He} has already, evidently, sampled it.

choices.text: Pour the plum wine for {npc} in the Hall, and hear the story again

effects.log: You pour it. The story improves with each telling, and the Hall of Offerings has a rare evening of gaiety.

choices.text: Confiscate the wine for the Feast and thank {npc} for the news

effects.log: You confiscate it. The Feast has an unusual warmth, and {npc} sulks, and forgives you.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with a question from the mortals, scrawled on a thousand scraps of bark: "are you listening?" It was left at a hundred shrines, in a hundred hands. {npc} has gathered them all. The pile is the size of a haystack. {He} has read them. {He} says they are not complaints. They are a kind of shy, collective hope.

choices.text: Answer the question, in a dream, to all who asked it

effects.log: You answer: "yes." It takes the night, and the district wakes with a vague, lasting gladness.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to carry the answer, in person, to each shrine, over a year

effects.log: {npc} goes. The year is long, and the answer, spoken by a herald, is received with tears, and {he} comes home thin and deeply content.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the road with a message that does not belong to you: a letter, sealed, addressed to the head of a far Lineage, entrusted to {him} by a dying stranger who then died. {npc} did not know what to do. {He} carried it three years. {He} asks whether you could advise. It is a very small letter, folded to the size of a coin.

choices.text: Send {npc} to deliver it to the Lineage, with your name on the carrying

effects.log: You send {him}. The letter, delivered, turns out to be a confession of a hundred years, and {npc} comes home a trusted friend of two Lineages.

choices.text: Open the letter, with {npc} as a witness, and decide

effects.log: You open it. It is a love letter, and a very old one, and you deliver it, in the end, with a note of your own.
